Question: Davis decided to kill Adams. He set out for Adams' house. Before he got there he saw Brooks, who resembled Adams. Thinking Brooks was Adams, Davis shot at Brooks. The shot missed Brooks but wounded Case, who was some distance away. Davis had not seen Case. In a prosecution under a statute that proscribes attempt to commit murder, the district attorney should indicate that the intended victim(s) was (were)

Options:
A. Adams only.
B. Brooks only.
C. Case only.
D. Adams and Brooks.

Please analyze the legal rules and select the correct option.

<Legal_Concept>
Attempted murder, specific intent, and target identification in criminal attempt.
</Legal_Concept>

<Fact_Analysis>
Davis intended to kill Adams, mistook Brooks for Adams, and fired a shot directly at Brooks. The shot missed Brooks and wounded an unseen bystander, Case.
</Fact_Analysis>

<Rule_Application>
Attempted murder requires specific intent to commit the crime against the person targeted at the scene of the act. When Davis targeted and fired at Brooks believing him to be Adams, his immediate intent and attempt were directed specifically at Brooks. Transferred intent does not apply to create an attempt on Case, nor does it shift the immediate target of the attempt back to Adams.
</Rule_Application>

<Legal_Conclusion>
The defendant's deliberate act of aiming and shooting was directed at the individual before him (Brooks). Therefore, in a prosecution for attempted murder based on that specific shooting, the intended victim was Brooks only. Option B is correct.
</Legal_Conclusion>

Question: Jack, a bank teller, was fired by Morgan, the president of the bank. Jack decided to take revenge against Morgan, but decided against attempting it personally, because he knew Morgan was protected around the clock by bank security guards. Jack knew that Chip had a violent temper and was very jealous. Jack falsely told Chip that Chip's wife, Elsie, was having an affair with Morgan. Enraged, Chip said, "What am I going to do?" Jack said, "If it were my wife, I'd just march into his office and blow his brains out." Chip grabbed a revolver and rushed to the bank. He walked into the bank, carrying the gun in his hand. One of the security guards, believing a holdup was about to occur, shot and killed Chip. If charged with murder of Chip, Jack should be found

Options:
A. guilty, based upon extreme recklessness.
B. guilty, based upon transferred intent.
C. not guilty, because he did not intend for Chip to be shot by the security guard.
D. not guilty, because he did not shoot Chip and he was not acting in concert with the security guard.

Please analyze the legal rules and select the correct option.

<Legal_Concept>
Depraved-heart / reckless murder and proximate causation.
</Legal_Concept>

<Fact_Analysis>
Jack manipulated Chip, a person with a known violent temper, with a inflammatory lie and coaxed him to enter a heavily guarded bank with a firearm, foreseeably inciting lethal force from security guards.
</Fact_Analysis>

<Rule_Application>
Common law murder includes killings resulting from conduct that manifests extreme indifference to human life (depraved-heart murder). Jack intentionally created a volatile, life-threatening environment where a violent outcome was highly foreseeable, establishing proximate cause and extreme recklessness.
</Rule_Application>

<Legal_Conclusion>
Jack acted with gross indifference to human life by engineering a predictable lethal confrontation, making him guilty of murder based on extreme recklessness. Option A is correct.
</Legal_Conclusion>

Question: Jack, a bank teller, was fired by Morgan, the president of the bank. Jack decided to take revenge against Morgan, but decided against attempting it personally, because he knew Morgan was protected around the clock by bank security guards. Jack knew that Chip had a violent temper and was very jealous. Jack falsely told Chip that Chip's wife, Elsie, was having an affair with Morgan. Enraged, Chip said, "What am I going to do?" Jack said, "If it were my wife, I'd just march into his office and blow his brains out." Chip grabbed a revolver and rushed to the bank. He walked into the bank, carrying the gun in his hand. One of the security guards, believing a holdup was about to occur, shot and killed Chip. If charged with attempted murder of Morgan, Jack should be found

Options:
A. guilty, because he intended to kill Morgan and used Chip to carry out his plan.
B. guilty, because he was extremely reckless as to Morgan.
C. not guilty, because Morgan was never in imminent danger of being killed.
D. not guilty, because Chip, if successful, would be guilty of no more than manslaughter and an accessory cannot be guilty of a higher crime than the principal.

Please analyze the legal rules and select the correct option.

<Legal_Concept>
Attempted murder and liability through an agent/instrument.
</Legal_Concept>

<Fact_Analysis>
Jack harbored specific intent to kill Morgan and manipulated Chip into acting as his instrument to execute the murder.
</Fact_Analysis>

<Rule_Application>
Attempted murder requires specific intent to kill along with an overt act beyond mere preparation toward executing that intent. A principal who uses an unwitting or incited agent to carry out a crime is liable for the criminal steps taken by that agent.
</Rule_Application>

<Legal_Conclusion>
Jack possessed the specific intent to kill Morgan and used Chip to carry out the attempt. Once Chip took substantial steps toward the killing by entering the bank armed, Jack became guilty of attempted murder. Option A is correct.
</Legal_Conclusion>

Question: Dobbs, while intoxicated, drove his car through a playground crowded with children just to watch the children run to try to get out of his way. His car struck one of the children, killing her instantly. Which of the following is the best theory for finding Dobbs guilty of murder?

Options:
A. Transferred intent
B. Felony murder, with assault with a deadly weapon as the underlying felony
C. Intentional killing, since he knew that the children were there and he deliberately drove his car at them
D. Commission of an act highly dangerous to life, without an intent to kill but with disregard of the consequences

Please analyze the legal rules and select the correct option.

<Legal_Concept>
Depraved-heart murder and extreme recklessness.
</Legal_Concept>

<Fact_Analysis>
Dobbs intentionally drove a vehicle through a playground crowded with children to scare them, resulting in the immediate death of a child.
</Fact_Analysis>

<Rule_Application>
Common law murder includes killings caused by acts committing wanton disregard for human life (depraved-heart murder). Specific intent to kill is not required; malice is implied from performing an act highly dangerous to human life with conscious disregard of the deadly risks.
</Rule_Application>

<Legal_Conclusion>
Driving through a crowded playground constitutes an act naturally dangerous to human life performed with complete disregard for consequences, providing the requisite malice for murder. Option D is correct.
</Legal_Conclusion>

Question: Sam decided to kill his boss, Anna, after she told him that he would be fired if his work did not improve. Sam knew Anna was scheduled to go on a business trip on Monday morning. On Sunday morning, Sam went to the company parking garage and put a bomb in the company car that Anna usually drove. The bomb was wired to go off when the car engine started. Sam then left town. At 5 a.m. Monday, Sam, after driving all night, was overcome with remorse and had a change of heart. He called the security officer on duty at the company and told him about the bomb. The security officer said he would take care of the matter. An hour later, the officer put a note on Anna's desk telling her of the message. He then looked at the car but could not see any signs of a bomb. He printed a sign saying "DO NOT USE THIS CAR," put it on the windshield, and went to call the police. Before the police arrived, Lois, a company vice president, got into the car and started the engine. The bomb went off, killing her. The jurisdiction defines murder in the first degree as any homicide committed with premeditation and deliberation or any murder in the commission of a common-law felony. Second-degree murder is defined as all other murder at common law. Manslaughter is defined by the common law. Sam is guilty of

Options:
A. murder in the first degree, because, with premeditation and deliberation, he killed whoever would start the car.
B. murder in the second degree, because he had no intention of killing Lois.
C. manslaughter, because at the time of the explosion, he had no intent to kill, and the death of Lois was in part the fault of the security officer.
D. only attempted murder of Anna, because the death of Lois was the result of the security officer's negligence.

Please analyze the legal rules and select the correct option.

<Legal_Concept>
First-degree premeditated murder, transferred intent, and ineffective withdrawal/abandonment.
</Legal_Concept>

<Fact_Analysis>
Sam premeditatedly planted an explosive device in a car to kill Anna. Despite later feelings of remorse, his efforts to stop the outcome failed, and Lois was killed when the bomb exploded.
</Fact_Analysis>

<Rule_Application>
When a defendant acts with premeditation and deliberation to kill one person, the doctrine of transferred intent transfers that mental state to any unintended victim killed by the act. Furthermore, withdrawal is ineffective as a defense once the dangerous instrumentality is set in motion unless the danger is fully neutralized prior to harm occurring.
</Rule_Application>

<Legal_Conclusion>
Sam acted with premeditation and deliberation when setting the bomb, and under transferred intent, this state of mind attaches to the death of Lois. Option A is correct.
</Legal_Conclusion>
